data.title: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
data.description: HONG KONG: Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the US tightens restrictions on China's access to the world's cutting-edge chips. Chinese tech giant Alibaba, which on Thursday (Nov 19)  announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new US rules could affect some of its global data centre expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions. The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation , following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centres in third countries, the latest US move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models. ALIBABA'S AI REVENUES SURGING AS DEMAND GROWS As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing US export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips. But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the US to close what some policymakers called a loophole. As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data centre investment plans in China and abroad. Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies. For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53 per cent year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan (US$9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10 per cent from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan (US$41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected. While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60 per cent during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan (US$7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.US CHIP CURB "SETS EVERYONE BACK IN CHINA": TENCENT Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new US rule on chip access "sets everyone back in China". “Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said. “Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS - Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new US rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute. A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a US think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centres could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster. Analysts expect the US will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised US national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that US officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies. Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new US rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas "economic coercion" . Analysts and industry leaders in China say the US’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient. “Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

data.title: Asian shares head for worst week since 2020 as AI trade gloom fails to abate
data.description: HONG KONG, Nov 20 : Asian shares slid on Friday to be on track for their worst week since 2020, as Anthropic's debut failed to restore investor faith in AI trades, while the dollar extended a rally on safe-haven flows. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares lost 2.5 per cent, poised for a six-day losing streak. The gauge has now declined 7 per cent this week, its worst performance since March 2020. Japan's Nikkei tumbled 4.1 per cent and was headed for a 6.8 per cent weekly drop, while South Korea's KOSPI fell 4.7 per cent and was set to end the week 7.5 per cent lower. The moves in Asia followed losses of more than 2 per cent for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite. Anthropic, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company, saw its shares surge more than 30 per cent in a historic debut but the euphoria failed to lift other boats. "Anthropic's blockbuster IPO proved not enough to assuage the overall concern about the outlook for the AI trade and equities more broadly," said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com. The wider AI sector has been bruised by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia as well as additional momentum for the anti-data-center movement in the wake of the Democrats' sweep of the US midterm elections. Unease about mounting debt loads in the sector and warnings that AI threatens human extinction have also hit sentiment. Rodda said that with the AI trade fading and Fed rate hikes seen likely, general market sentiment is shaky and the risk is that this bearishness begins to drag stocks even lower. US stock futures also point to further losses, with the S&P 500 futures down 0.4 per cent and Nasdaq futures down 0.7 per cent in Asia on Friday. DOLLAR EXTENDS RALLY, TREASURY YIELDS DIP ON RISK AVERSION As risk sentiment took a beating, the US dollar extended its rally, also supported by growing expectations of a more hawkish Federal Reserve. The dollar index last traded steady at 103.86, after hitting its strongest level since April 2025 this week. Fed funds futures imply that a quarter-point rate hike next month is essentially locked in, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. In government debt, US Treasury yields eased as the sharp equity selloff pushed investors toward safe-haven bonds. The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes held steady at 5.026 per cent, near a one-week low. The two-year yield touched 4.749 per cent, compared with a US close of 4.779 per cent. Oil prices were mostly steady after an earlier spike, as reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offset pressure from rising US crude inventories and forecasts for a global oil surplus. Brent crude futures settled flat at $91.98 a barrel, on track for a third straight week of decline. Non-interest-bearing gold dipped 0.6 per cent to $3,601.40 an ounce and was headed for a 7.3 per cent weekly loss.

data.title: Oil prices set for third straight weekly decline on Middle East export flows
data.description: LONDON - Nov 20 : Oil prices edged down on Friday and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.     Brent crude futures were down 95 cents, or 1 per cent, to $91.03 a barrel at 0900 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December were down $1.40, or 1.7 per cent, to $81.81 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down 83 cents, or 1 per cent, to $81.61. Brent is on track for a 5 per cent decline for the week and the December WTI contract for an almost 8 per cent weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline. "This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of the Middle East. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there's a deal in the making," said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas. "The prices are correct if you believe that this geopolitical risk doesn't come back. I'm not in that camp who thinks this is done... I probably see a rebound," he said. The Iran-aligned Houthi movement fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and "are burning", Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday. Iran's intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, "running at roughly one incident per day in November", still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4 per cent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency said on Thursday. However, some analysts expect softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday — heading for their worst week since 2020. "Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices," said Saxo analysts in a note. In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45 per cent since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

data.title: Analysis:BOJ's ambiguity on rate hike path could tempt yen bears
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 20 : Bank of Japan policymakers mostly agree on the need for an interest rate hike next month, but their split over how far rates should eventually rise risks muddying the outlook and triggering a fresh round of yen selling. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has struggled at times to get his hawkish signals across to markets, including in December last year, when the yen fell despite the decision then to hike rates. While vague messaging helps the BOJ keep its options open amid heightened economic uncertainty, the lack of clarity on how far the bank could eventually raise rates has also become a particular trigger for yen bears. A board reshuffle next year, which gives Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi a chance to replace two departing hawks with her preferred candidates, may also shift the debate around the terminal rate - now seen by markets at around 1.75 per cent to 2 per cent, analysts say. That uncertainty could undermine any messages by Ueda that steady rate hikes were on the horizon as the bank focuses on mounting price pressures, analysts say. "The BOJ may be hoping to avoid giving too clear a guidance on the pace of rate hikes, as it's their first experience seeking to anchor inflation around its 2 per cent target," said Mari Iwashita, executive rates strategist at Nomura Securities. "But sustained US rate hikes would keep the BOJ under pressure to raise rates too," in order to prevent US-Japan rate differentials from widening too much and triggering yen falls, she said. AMBIGUITY DISCOUNT Ueda last month declared inflation had reached the BOJ's 2 per cent target and stressed a shift in phase towards policy that focuses on fighting inflation risks with steady rate hikes. Speaking in parliament on Thursday, Ueda shrugged off recent soft signs in consumption as temporary and projected spending to recover, cementing the chance of a December rate hike. What is less clear is the pace and timing of rate hikes next year with recent commentary from BOJ policymakers showing a divergence in their views on how far its policy rate - now at 1.25 per cent - is from levels deemed neutral to the economy. While BOJ staff estimates place Japan's nominal neutral rate in a range of 1.1 per cent to 2.5 per cent, there is no consensus within the board on where within the band the neutral rate lies. Hawkish board member Naoki Tamura projected the neutral rate to be around 2 per cent. Another hawk, Hajime Takata, said on Monday the BOJ must raise rates to a "good" position, which he described as near the middle of the estimated 1.1 per cent-2.5 per cent range. Others seen by markets as holding the casting vote on the rate-hike timing are less sure. Former academic Junko Koeda has said only the neutral rate was "likely significantly above 1 per cent." Kazuyuki Masu has not given any projection on the neutral rate but stressed in September the need to pull real interest rates out of negative territory as soon as possible. Doves, on the other hand, see less scope for further hikes, signalling the policy rate may already be close to neutral. Toichiro Asada said last week Japan's neutral rate was "not necessarily high," while Ayano Sato cited weak consumption as a reason for voting against the September hike. YEN HOLDS KEY A majority of economists polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.5 per cent in December, followed by another hike by end-March. They see the terminal rate to be around 1.75 per cent or 2 per cent. Ueda and his two deputies have done little to give markets clarity, staying mum on the neutral level and saying only that loose financial conditions leave scope for continued rate hikes. The ambiguity reflects the difficulty predicting how households and firms, accustomed to prolonged ultra-low rates, react to steadily rising borrowing costs. Even the hawks have held off on proposing aggressive tightening measures. Takata, for one, said the BOJ must avoid being bound by particular intervals in raising rates and take a nimble, data-dependent approach. Some lawmakers who grilled Ueda in parliament on Thursday questioned his view that consumption will recover, a sign of the political heat the BOJ may face in steering further rate hikes. While Takaichi has said little on the BOJ's rate-hike plans, she will have the chance to fill openings in the nine-member board when the two hawks, Tamura and Takata, see their terms expire in July next year. The seat now occupied by former banker Tamura may go to a conservative megabank executive, however, the other opening may be filled by a candidate less hawkish than Takata, analysts say. In the end, yen moves will be key to how far the BOJ will raise rates, said veteran BOJ watcher Katsutoshi Inadome, who projects rates to move up to 2.0 per cent next year - or even to 2.25 per cent around the summer if the yen continues to weaken. "Given so many moving parts, maybe it's inevitable the BOJ's message becomes ambiguous," said Inadome, who is senior strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset ​Management. "But if the yen's weakness persists, the BOJ will have little choice but to keep hiking steadily. I also wonder whether Takaichi would do anything that would push down the yen."

data.title: Exclusive-Signal restricts screenshots to block AI agents from reading messages
data.description: NEW YORK, Nov 20 : Encrypted messaging service Signal said on Friday it would restrict screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats on phones, warning that the tech industry's push to embed AI in consumer devices was eroding its ability to guarantee privacy. Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly. The move reflects growing tension between privacy-focused apps and the biggest tech companies, which are racing to roll out AI agents designed to see what is on a user's screen and take actions based on it. Signal identified as particularly worrisome the AI capabilities built directly into operating systems, like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence, because of how deeply they are integrated into people's devices. Operating systems maintain the environment in which Signal and other applications must exist, the company said. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post provided to Reuters ahead of its release on Signal's website. To prevent agents from scanning Signal messages, the service is introducing new settings blocking screenshot access on people's phones and switching those restrictions on by default. Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.      GETTING AROUND PROTECTIONS Agents that can take actions on behalf of users are billed as the next big wave of AI technology, capable of surfacing relevant information from across different apps and executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases autonomously, without direct instructions. However, that reach can get around the protections that apps like Signal build for themselves. Reuters reported earlier this week that Meta's Muse agent was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to access Signal messages on both an Apple computer and a phone using Google's Android system. In both cases, Muse used broad operating system-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull in the messages, using those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate. On Apple's macOS, for instance, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers for people with disabilities to navigate over to Signal, take screenshots of chats there, extract text from those pictures and reproduce the messages inside the Muse app. An operating system update from Apple this week effectively closed that specific pathway, but also introduced a new set of permissions aimed at agents that offers similar capabilities paired with additional user warnings. Meta said in response to Reuters' reporting that agents need to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and that Muse can access other apps only via permissions users explicitly grant. Signal said that developers should have straightforward ways of opting their apps out of such data processing by AI assistants entirely, specifically mentioning screen reading, notifications and other file system access. The service, owned by a non-profit foundation, promises its users a secure messaging experience by limiting the data it stores on its own servers, eschewing ads and offering end-to-end encryption, meaning it cannot access and read the conversations conducted on its app. AI systems that scan people's screens can undermine those protections by pulling the messages out of Signal's secure environment and into whatever other servers the agent is using, it said in the post.

data.title: Equinor says cyberattack against company has been stopped
data.description: COPENHAGEN, Nov 20 : Norwegian oil and gas group Equinor said a cyberattack against the company had been stopped as of Friday, adding there had been no impact to production and there was no indication data had been stolen or altered. • Europe's largest gas supplier said on Tuesday it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some IT systems • "There is also no indication that the attack has had any negative consequences for employees, partners or suppliers," Equinor said in a statement on Friday • The incident has been reported to the police, it added

data.title: Japan's core inflation accelerates in October, cementing rate hike expectations
data.description: TOKYO: Japan's annual core inflation accelerated in October and exceeded the central bank's 2 per cent target for the second straight month, a sign of broadening price pressures that cements the case for a near-term interest rate. The data will be among factors the Bank of Japan will scrutinise at its next two-day policy meeting ending on Dec 18, when many market players expect the central bank to hike its policy rate to 1.5 per cent from the current 1.25 per cent. In a sign the government may not oppose a near-term rate rise, Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi blamed data on Monday showing weak consumption last quarter on temporary factors and projected rising wages to underpin household income. "We see signs the economy is moving closer toward a desirable state, in which wages and prices rise stably in tandem," Kiuchi told a news briefing on Friday. The core consumer price index (CPI), which strips away the effect of volatile fresh food, rose 2.2 per cent in October from a year earlier, data showed on Friday, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3 per cent gain. It followed a 2.1 per cent rise in September. An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.2 per cent in October from a year earlier after increasing 2.4 per cent in September. While food inflation slowed to 2.2 per cent in October from a 2.9 per cent jump in September, prices increased for a broad range of daily necessities, the data showed, a sign firms kept passing on rising costs from the Middle East conflict and the weak yen. Goods prices were up 3.2 per cent year-on-year in October, faster than a 2.8 per cent gain in September and a 1.4 per cent rise in services prices, suggesting that inflation was still driven by high raw material costs rather than wage pressures. Many analysts expect prices to rise more quickly in coming months, as persistent yen falls and the prolonged Middle East war push up the cost of importing fuel and raw material. "Consumer inflation is likely to accelerate sharply at the outset of next year," said Takeshi Minami, chief economist at Norinchukin Research Institute. "The BOJ has signalled its resolve to keep rising rates, so there's a strong chance it will hike in December. It could also contemplate another hike in March 2027 when inflation is likely to exceed 3 per cent," he said. MARKET VOLATILITY A RISK With high energy and import prices adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept interest rates steady last month but stressed its policy has entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot, reinforcing its hawkish bias. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates in December and follow up with another by end-March. Critics of the BOJ's rate-hike plans have pointed to data showing Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in the third quarter, with weak consumption overshadowing robust corporate activity. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda on Thursday played down the soft consumption data and projected household spending will recover, bolstering the case for a rate hike as soon as next month. A complication that may prompt the BOJ to hold off on a December hike is market volatility with concern over AI returns triggering a sell-off in tech shares, some analysts say. "The big picture hasn't changed. Inflation is on course to accelerate and brisk corporate activity will keep Japan's economy on a moderate recovery path," said Yoshiki Shinke, senior executive economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute. "But if markets remain unstable, the BOJ may prefer to stand pat next month. If the US Federal Reserve opts to hike in December, however, the BOJ will face a tough choice."

data.title: Analysis:Anthropic listing extends Nasdaq's dominant run against arch-rival NYSE
data.description: NEW YORK, Nov 19 : The market share battle between the two top US exchanges has never been so lopsided. With Anthropic's record-breaking initial public offering on Wednesday, Nasdaq snatched another marquee listing from the New York Stock Exchange this year, adding to its already wide lead in the battle for market share against its downtown rival. The exchange displayed the Anthropic win on the huge screens that envelop its Times Square address on Thursday, as more than 800 million shares changed hands in the AI company's debut. "Anthropic’s IPO is a very proud moment for us," said Adena Friedman, chief executive officer of Nasdaq, in an interview Thursday. "We’ve been engaging with the Anthropic team for a very long time. Separate from the entire listing experience, we've been a client to them, as we are to the AI ecosystem, and so we also have gotten to know them in that context as well." Over the last decade, the listing advantage has swung decisively in Nasdaq's favor. According to data from Dealogic, there have been 64 IPOs — led by Anthropic and SpaceX — on Nasdaq so far this year, raising about $201.8 billion, dwarfing the $20.8 billion haul raised from 42 IPOs on NYSE. That is the widest gap in terms of capital raised between the two exchanges record since Dealogic started tracking the data in 1995. In 2017, NYSE raked in share sale proceeds of $28.8 billion from 69 deals, versus Nasdaq's $9.3 billion haul from 86 flotations. However, Nasdaq finished ahead of NYSE six out of eight times between 2018 and 2025, according to Dealogic, and is on track to do so again this year. Nasdaq’s run of dominance can be linked to several moves the exchange operator has made over the years. Friedman, who has led Nasdaq for a decade, on Thursday cited the exchange operator's strength in marketing IPOs, its investor relations business that helps connect companies with large asset managers and institutional investors, and its index business — which it launched in 1985 — as key competitive advantages. These efforts have allowed it to build relationships with founders in big IPO hubs like Silicon Valley and contributed to its dominance in tech listings. "It's a very hard problem (for NYSE) to solve because Nasdaq didn't build its private markets business or its index just two years ago. They have had a head start of several years compared to their competitors. NYSE will have to probably just copy what Nasdaq has done for the past 10 years," said Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street. NYSE executives are under increasing pressure to win the next mega-IPO after the recent losses to Nasdaq, according to two people familiar with the matter. The NYSE did not respond to a request for comment. "Probably the major reason (for their dominance) is that Nasdaq has their own indexes," said Lau, referring to the Nasdaq 100 and the Nasdaq Composite, which are licensed for use by institutional asset managers. "That is a very big draw for many companies such as SpaceX and Anthropic." The Nasdaq 100's constituents include several of the world's most valuable companies, such as Apple, Nvidia and Alphabet. STRATEGIC ADVANTAGE Admission to benchmarks like the Nasdaq 100 or S&P 500 gives companies increased access to deep-pocketed institutions with large index funds. This broadens the companies' shareholder base and improves share liquidity. The NYSE has a similar index that tracks its 100 largest US stocks that it launched last year, but it is less widely followed by investors. Nasdaq introduced new rules earlier this year to speed the addition of newly listed megacap companies to the index, a move experts say gives them another advantage over the NYSE, even as it has drawn criticism from some quarters. In an interview with Bloomberg in May, NYSE President Lynn Martin called the rule changes "questionable." On Thursday, Friedman said only a handful of megacap companies of the size and scale of Anthropic and SpaceX have the potential to be fast-tracked into the Nasdaq 100, adding that market liquidity is not an issue. Reuters reported in March that SpaceX made early inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 a necessary condition to list on the Nasdaq. The exchange ultimately added the company to the index 15 days after its stock market debut.

data.title: Alibaba defrauded shareholders by concealing ties to suspected spy in Nvidia scandal, lawsuit says
data.description: NEW YORK, Nov 19 : Alibaba was sued on Thursday in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation last week. According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business. Shareholders cited Alibaba's relationship with Megaspeed, a ​Singaporean company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia AI chips, and whose executive Alice Huang had a relationship with Jensen Huang, who is not related to her. The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14 per cent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba's ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed's "dominant" customer. They attributed part of the decline to a November 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia's spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies' remote use of ‌advanced processors. Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant. Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors. Wu said on Thursday that Alibaba remained on track for $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20 per cent EBITDA margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company's products and services next year. The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia. In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of "Chinese military companies" that the Department of Defense linked to that country's military. Last month, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon ​contracts to companies whose lobbyists also work with designated Chinese military companies. Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government. Thursday's lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba's American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and November 11, 2026.

data.title: Japan says JT dividend cut will not disrupt government's industrial investment
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 20 : Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday that the government's industrial investment programme would not be affected by Japan Tobacco's decision to cut its dividend following the loss of control of its Russian business. The government owns a 37.55 per cent stake in Japan Tobacco and uses dividend income from the cigarette maker as a source of funding for industrial investment. "Even after the revision to the dividend forecast, there is no possibility that industrial investment will be hindered," Katayama told a regular news conference. The Japanese government booked 156 billion yen ($977.02 million) in income from its JT holdings into its special account for the year ended in March. Japan Tobacco said on Thursday it would record a loss and lowered its annual dividend forecast by 25 per cent after losing control of its Russian subsidiaries when President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure this month. The Russian units, which had accounted for around 25 per cent of group profits, will no longer be included in its consolidated earnings, the company said. Shares of Japan Tobacco slumped 10.1 per cent on Friday, losing more than 30 per cent since the Russian business seizure. Tokyo has protested through diplomatic channels and requested that the Russian seizure be withdrawn. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Thursday that she raised the JT issue during talks with Putin in Shenzhen. "We had an in-depth discussion and the necessary exchanges. The biggest step forward was establishing an environment in which we can communicate directly in the future," she said. ($1 = 159.6700 yen)

data.title: Oil prices gain as Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise supply concerns
data.description: Nov 20 : Oil prices rose on Friday but were set for a weekly decline as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.     Brent crude futures rose 79 cents, or 0.9 per cent, to $92.77 a barrel by 0404 GMT. "Expectations that coordinated production cuts will continue at the OPEC+ meeting later this month are also providing support," he said. The Iran-aligned Houthi movement fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Houthis. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4 per cent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday. However, some analysts were still expecting softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday - heading for their worst week since 2020. "Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices," said Saxo analysts in a note. Separately, in Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45 per cent since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

data.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
data.description: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company. The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion . That kind of number was once unheard of for a company's first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth - and most recently the AI boom - has changed that. Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars (following SpaceX just months ago), and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits. Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology's risks overall. Here are some numbers to help understand Thursday's IPO. The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday's (Nov 19) trading, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each , putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June. The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix (US$26.5 billion in July) and oil giant Saudi Aramco (US$25.6 billion in 2019). Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion The initial price per share was set at US$83. But that spiked more than 30 per cent to open at US$111.50 a share - pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon. By market close on Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That's still over 17 per cent higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly US$1.75 trillion. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion.Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11 Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S&P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018. How far a trillion US dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 156 million km That would surpass the roughly 150 million km between Earth and the sun. The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million. There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122.

data.title: Asian stocks plunge as Anthropic fails to dispel AI fears
data.description: TOKYO: Japanese and South Korean stocks plunged in early trade on Friday (Nov 20) after chip-related stocks fell on Wall Street , despite the stellar debut performance of Anthropic. At around 9.35am (8.35am Singapore time) the Nikkei 225 was down 4.02 per cent at 57,051.43 points, while South Korea's benchmark Kospi index fell 3.81 per cent to 4,942.22 points. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, raised a record US$81.3 billion in its initial offering, with shares closing 17 per cent higher in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday. But the gain came on a rough day for markets, with both the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the broader S&P 500 closing down more than 2 per cent.  The record IPO also failed to settle nerves on trading floors as they deal with the fallout from the crisis engulfing AI titan Nvidia. Online brokerage Monex said that given the strength of demand for Anthropic stock, "some people have suggested that there may even be a shift of funds away from high-tech stocks" in order to buy the company's newly listed shares.

data.title: Japan says JT dividend cut will not disrupt government's industrial investment plans
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 20 : Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday that the government's industrial investment programme would not be affected by Japan Tobacco's decision to cut its dividend following the loss of control of its Russian business. The government owns a 37.55 per cent stake in Japan Tobacco and uses dividend income from the cigarette maker as a source of funding for industrial investment. "Even after the revision to the dividend forecast, there is no possibility that industrial investment will be hindered," Katayama told a regular news conference. Japan Tobacco said on Thursday it will record a loss and lowered its annual dividend forecast by 25 per cent after losing control of its Russian subsidiaries when President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure this month. The Russian units, which had accounted for around 25 per cent of group profits, will no longer be included in its consolidated earnings, the company said. Shares of Japan Tobacco slumped more than 8 per cent early on Friday. The Japanese government booked 156 billion yen ($977.02 million) in income from its JT holdings into its special account for the year ended in March. ($1 = 159.6700 yen)
